discussion_why: More of a delightful whimsical toy than a hot debate topic, though it does spark 'is the swarm one mind or many' chatter.

discussion_why: More of a 'huh, neat' science-explainer than a betting/poker discussion driver.

title: The AI Scientist That Discovered a Protein Law Nobody Knew
paper: 2504.19017v1 - Sparks: Multi-Agent AI Discovers Protein Design Principles

discussion_why: Rides the 'will AI replace scientists' debate, which tends to spill into prediction-market/betting chat about AGI timelines.

title: Generator-Critic Agent Pair for Poker Range Design

discussion_why: Directly merges the hot 'AI agents doing autonomous discovery' trend with poker strategy, a natural discord flashpoint over whether AI can find genuinely new exploits.

title: De Bruijn Deck — the card trick that's secretly a colored k-mer graph
pitch: An interactive HTML page that builds a classic self-working 'mind-reading' card trick from a de Bruijn sequence, then lets you toggle a graph view showing the exact k-mer/de Bruijn graph structure (the same combinatorial object the paper surveys for pangenomics) that makes the trick work.
discussion_why: Wins on whimsy — a real magic trick that's provably just graph theory is the kind of thing people can't resist testing on friends.

title: Solver Line Fingerprinter
pitch: Apply colored de Bruijn graph indexing (built for finding shared substrings across many colored genomes) to poker solver output libraries or hand-history databases, to detect near-duplicate lines/ranges reused across solvers or players.
discussion_why: Fits the poker/ai axis — 'is this solver line actually novel or a copy of a known GTO output' is a live argument in study-group Discords.

title: The Data Structure Hiding in Both Pangenomes and Card Tricks
pitch: An explainer connecting colored de Bruijn graphs (bioinformatics' tool for indexing many genomes at once) to the magician's de Bruijn sequence trick — same math, wildly different costumes.
discussion_why: Wins on surprise — most people have no idea genomics and card magic run on the identical data structure.

title: Antbook — live-odds ant races
pitch: Simulate several ants using the paper's fitted active-Brownian + run-and-tumble parameters (real turn-angle, run-time, and waiting-time distributions from lab data) racing toward a food source, with a live odds board users bet fake chips against as the swarm's positions update.
discussion_why: Wins on betting/whimsy fusion — it's literally a sportsbook built on peer-reviewed insect kinematics, an easy 'wait, this is real data?' hook.

title: Random Walk Zoo
pitch: Side-by-side interactive canvas comparing active Brownian motion, run-and-tumble, and Levy-flight walkers with sliders for turn-angle spread, run time, and waiting time, so you can feel why 'randomness' isn't a single thing.
discussion_why: Wins on math surprise — sliders make the abstract difference between walk types visually obvious in seconds.

title: Why an Ant's Random Walk Is Basically a Slot Machine
pitch: Explainer using the ant movement model's run-time/waiting-time distributions to teach variance and expected-value intuition, drawing a direct line to payout distributions in gambling.
discussion_why: Wins on gambling relevance — reframing insect locomotion stats as slot-machine variance is a sharp, discussable analogy.

title: Organic NPC swarm-movement library
pitch: Package the paper's empirically-fit turn-angle/run-time/waiting-time distributions as a drop-in game-dev crowd/creature AI movement module, more lifelike than typical Perlin-noise wander behaviors.
discussion_why: Wins on niche buildability appeal for game devs wanting cheap realism upgrades over generic noise-based wandering.

title: Go or Grow — an evolutionary game sandbox
pitch: A replicator-dynamics simulator where you set payoffs for 'stay & proliferate' vs 'migrate & seek resources,' watch a cell population evolve live toward a mixed evolutionarily-stable strategy, with the paper's BAP1-mutation renal-cancer scenario as a preset.
discussion_why: Wins on decision-theory crossover — watching a mixed ESS emerge live is the same visual you'd want for explaining GTO bluff frequencies.

title: Your Poker Strategy Is Also How Cancer Spreads
pitch: Walk through the paper's evolutionary game (ESS, mixed strategies, coexistence of primary/metastatic tumor populations) and draw the direct parallel to mixed-strategy equilibria in poker — bluff frequencies, range balancing, GTO solves.
discussion_why: Wins on poker relevance — a legitimate biology paper independently re-deriving 'balanced mixed strategies win' is catnip for a poker-strategy Discord argument.

title: Replicator Dynamics Toolkit
pitch: Generalize the paper's static evolutionary game solver into a reusable web library/CLI for computing ESS and simulating replicator dynamics on any 2-strategy payoff matrix — usable for teaching game theory or modeling population-level bet-sizing strategy drift in a betting market.
discussion_why: Wins on math generality — a clean reusable ESS solver is the kind of tool that gets reused across totally different debates (biology, betting, evolution of strategy).

title: The AI Scientist That Discovers Catalysts — and Why the Model Barely Matters
pitch: Explainer/reaction video on CatDT's central claim: an 8-agent, 27-tool digital twin outperforms raw LLM capability because of engineered harness — deterministic tools, persistent memory, and a self-improvement loop that lifted barrier-calculation success from 41% to 84%.
discussion_why: Wins on ai-discussion — 'the harness matters more than the model' is exactly the debate agent-builders are already having, now with hard numbers.

title: Memory-augmented retry loop, extracted
pitch: Pull out the paper's core trick — persistent memory across agent retries that turns a 41% success rate into 84% — into a small, domain-independent library usable for any agent pipeline with a verifiable pass/fail signal (bug-fix agents, backtest-tuning agents, etc.).
discussion_why: Wins on ai/decision-theory — a portable 'retry with memory' pattern is directly reusable in anyone's own agent-orchestration setup.

title: Digital Twin Labs — catalyst discovery as a service
pitch: Vertical SaaS offering self-evolving multi-agent digital twins for mid-size chemical/battery/hydrogen companies that can't afford in-house computational chemistry teams, specializing narrowly in heterogeneous catalysis rather than competing broadly with big AI4Science platforms.
discussion_why: Wins on econ framing — a narrow wedge into a real, underserved R&D cost problem is a concrete business debate, if a slow-buildable one.

title: Break the Rules Turbulence
pitch: A stylized 2D canvas simulation of chaotic polymer-flow ('elastic turbulence') patterns with a toggle for enforcing positive-definiteness vs letting the simulation locally drift unphysical — visually showing the paper's punchline that large-scale statistics look identical either way.
discussion_why: Wins on decision-theory surprise — 'breaking the local rules doesn't ruin the global outcome' is the exact process-vs-outcome debate poker players have about bad process/good result hands.

title: The Chaotic Beauty of Honey-Slow Turbulence (and Why Cheating the Math Doesn't Break It)
pitch: A visual explainer on elastic turbulence's psychedelic flow patterns in polymer solutions, paired with the paper's surprising finding that simulations violating a core physical constraint still match fully valid ones statistically.
discussion_why: Wins on whimsy — the flow patterns themselves are hypnotic and unfamiliar to most viewers, giving instant visual hook.

title: WebGL polymer-flow teaching applet
pitch: A polished, lightweight browser-based fluid dynamics teaching tool generalizing the elastic-turbulence demo into a reusable applet for physics courses covering non-Newtonian/viscoelastic flow.
discussion_why: Wins on buildability as a straightforward, self-contained educational visualization with modest but real classroom utility.
